newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House leaders say Republicans united.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House leaders say Republicans united.

text.p: U.S. House Republican leaders Wednesday said the rank-and-file remains united behind their leadership after a lengthy closed meeting to discuss concerns raised by many on the handling of recent legislation.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich told reporters the lawmakers had "a very long and helpful session." The 2-1/2 hour meeting was prompted by frustrations expressed by consevative lawmakers on the handling of the disaster relief bill.
The Georgia Republican told reporters, "This conference is very united," and added that their strategy on the tax bill will be to emphasize a simple message of tax relief.
"We are going to keep talking about cutting taxes rather than increasing welfare. We are going to keep very steady and very simple in the things we say and do," Gingrich told reporters.

The White House has been highly critical of the House Republican tax bill because its child tax credit would not benefit lower income families who pay little or no tax and certain tax benefits for child care would be less valuable.

However, House Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer said his tax bill will be modified to allow families earning below $50,000 a year to benefit from both the child care tax credit and the $500 a year child credit.
Archer said he was optimistic the $85 billion five-year tax cut would pass with bipartisan support.

He also expected the ethanol tax break to be extended not beyond 2000. Calling it "an anachronism and unjustified tax subsidy," the Texas Republican said, "It is due to expire. It is going to expire."

Tuesday, a group of conservative Republicans met to discuss their concerns that Republican leaders had been beaten badly by the White House in the public relations fight swirling around Clinton's veto of the disaster aid bill. It eventually passed after Republicans removed two provisions unrelated to the aid which he had not wanted.

House Majority Leader Dick Armey said the spending and tax cut legislation that clears Congress will be in compliance with the five-year balanced budget. He dismissed as a misunderstanding reports of his comments that he was not bound to uphold the agreement because it applied only to those who were in the room while it was being negotiated.

Gingrich noted that Armey was part of the negotiations and held out Vice President Al Gore as one who was not in on the talks and was now trying to move the budget to spend more liberally than the White House and Republican leaders had wanted.
